pr_title: Teach Command Palette to filter out duplicate command lines
pr_comments:
Spent tons of time on trying to remove code duplication, by
1. Creating an iterator that removes duplicates
2. Applying an "internal iterator" DP (to remove duplicates and call a consumer)

The solutions I have got were either inefficient or less readable.

I love that this uses hstring -- it's reference-counted so we're not wasting time copying strings all over the place just to unique them!

BTW Quite ironically a `std::set` can outperform `std::unordered_set` here on lower end hardware - I measured! 😄
The former allows us to only partially compare strings, whereas the latter will always hash arguments prematurely. Since our commands are likely to be short, hashing is faster than comparing....
...if MSVC had a good hash function, but it uses FNV1a, which isn't.

In either case we should stick with `std::unordered_set` here, but in the distant future it might be nice to migrate our hashmaps over to `martinus/robin-hood-hashing`. 😄

**NB** I haven't profiled this particular case so I could be completely wrong. Also this is way off the hot loop so I doubt performance even matters at all in this case with any reasonable choice.

With that said, if the full deduplication is left in, in general since we have so few things I am willing to bet that a plain linear scan over a std::vector will be faster than a fancier algorithm or data structure.

I guess the plain linear scan you are addressing is O(n^2), and it can still be more efficient then allocating the unordered set. Yet this balance changes at some point. And I actually prefer to use the cleaner solution. In any case we are discussing the efficiency of in-memory deduplication (measured in microseconds), while this is immediately followed by execution of command, that usually spawns another process, creates and renders brand new session (measured in seconds)

The deduplication of 20 items with `std::unordered_set` occurs within about 1600ns on a Ryzen 5 CPU. It's about 4x as much on what could be considered a lowest-end system. It's about 700ns with `martinus/robin-hood-hashing`. I believe this is sufficient for this feature. 🙂 We can still merge cool improvements of course, but I don't believe we have to.

Absolutely, I am aware of how inconsequential such a change is here. I just took an unneeded opportunity to be pedantic about how linear scan can be better than something that is O(log n) when you take constants into consideration.

review_comments: On saving I don't think you need to deduplicate everything and have a separate `uniqueCommands`. All you have to do is create the one output vector, add the new command, and then add in commands from `RecentCommands` where they are not equal to the current command.

In one of the previous comments @lhecker  suggested to remove deduplication when reading :smile:
I personally prefer to prefer to preserve deduplication in both cases, as IMHO it is a safer programming, usually providing better future compatibility.
Removed the deduplication from loading commands, preserving it here.

I prefered to leave the full deduplication for:

1. Backward compatibility (for those in preview who already have duplicate commands) (probably a corner case)
~2. Case where there are several terminals writing the same command~ (I guess this one is incorrect)

It's _theoretically_ possible for the existing commands list to contain duplicates, but this can only occur if the program was misbehaving and then all bets are off, wouldn't they?
I'm fine with the full deduplication, but technically @Rosefield's code is just as fine IMHO.
It is unfortunately difficult to convey things in text. I think that this is great overall, I just thought I saw a case where things could be simplified.

Yeah.. conveying things in text sucks! :blush: I try to use emoji - but it is still challenging 🤷 

I absolutely agree that @Rosefield's code is great as well! It is more a matter of taste: some "extra safety" at a price of some in memory checks. Given that this code is invoked only once upon user interaction which is slow by definition, I preferred to pay this price.
